text: Bai Ganyo, having finally convinced himself that there was no possibility of lodging with Irechek, picked up his saddlebags, paying no heed to the host’s entreaties to leave them at his house until he found accommodation, and set off, accompanied by the servant, for Nàrodny Kavàrna — the café where Bulgarian students gathered. It was already seven o’clock when he entered the café with the saddlebags in his hand and his kalpak on his head. You’d never guess who he was or where he came from! To the left of the entrance, around a table, sat several Bulgarian students.

One of them saw the incoming compatriot and nudged the others: “A Bulgarian, a Bulgarian!” Everyone turned at the moment when Bay Ganyo stopped a waiter carrying a tray of coffees and, trying as much as possible to distort the Bulgarian words so as to make them understandable to the foreigner, asked in a loud voice: “Where here Bulgarian little boys?” — and accompanied the question with a movement of his head and free hand. A burst of laughter from the left side put an end to the waiter’s bewilderment. Bay Ganyo turned and recognized his dark-eyed, dark-haired, huddled compatriots.

— Oh! Good day! Have you been here? — he cried heartily, set down the saddlebags, and began to seize the students’ hands. — Why are you looking at me? Don’t be afraid, I’m Bulgarian... Make room for me to sit down.
— What is your name, sir? — one of the students asked curiously.
— Me? Why do you ask? Ganyo Balkanski. I brought a little rose oil to your Prague — here it is in the saddlebag.
— Is that so? — cried one of the younger students in patriotic ecstasy. — Come on, let us see it.
He had really only heard of rose oil.
— What are you going to look at in it, oil is oil — replied Bay Ganyo, — it’s not for you. Leave the oil alone and tell me something else: where am I to settle down? I was just at Bay Irechek’s...
— So? — cried the exalted student again.

— “What do you mean, ‘so’?” Why shouldn’t I go to him? I went — I thought he’d show some human decency and invite me to his home as a guest. That faith! “My place is too cramped,” he says, “and I don’t know what else, I don’t know what.” He loves, he says, Bulgarians... Him! When there’s profit to be had, old Ganyo knows how to “love” too. — Is that how you welcome a Bulgarian? A Bulgarian!... Not to lie to you, the man fed me. And what a meal it was — well, let’s just say, it was enough to choke on!... Where are Bulgarians more hospitable; a Bulgarian, even if he has only one room, will still invite you...

Some of the students began to realize where Bay Ganyo was heading and were waiting from one minute to the next for him to show his hand. Only the exalted student responded sympathetically to his words and openly shared his indignation at the foreigners’ lack of hospitality.
— Indeed, our Bulgarians are very hospitable — he confirmed with the utmost confidence, — the locals don’t want to know you. We’re just lingering here in the cafés...

The student who uttered those words was very advanced in civilization, but for some reason he did not enjoy any particular reputation among his comrades; it seems that some sins weighed on his soul; among other things, people said that he was very fond of “making a quick profit.” No wonder! That accursed sin—miserliness—through the contagion of the surrounding domestic environment takes root almost from childhood; it dries out the soul of the young man, turning him into the coldest egoist: nothing tender, nothing noble remains in him. Material interest governs all the miser’s actions and determines his relations with those around him: no moral impulse precedes, no remorse follows his actions, which, without regard for the means, are directed toward gaining advantage. Even when those actions bring misfortune or shame to someone, even then, instead of pangs of conscience, the selfish miser feels satisfaction, as if others’ loss were his gain, others’ misfortune his happiness. Only one thing would disturb our young egoist—to be outwitted by someone. When in other nations the word “cunning” is synonymous with sly, treacherous, and, when attached to a person, would lower him in society’s esteem, among us the epithet cunning is worn like the most honorable decoration: “Well! What a clever boy he turned out to be, may his father live long, he fooled us all! We couldn’t deceive him! Bravo. Well done!”

No actions or relationships meant anything to Bodkov — that was his name — unless something tangible, some profit, came out of them. (Are there words in the European languages corresponding to these, in this sense?) If he visited the local families, he did not do so out of sociability or a desire to become acquainted with the way of life in more civilized circles; the intellectual and moral interests of that society not only did not engage him, but were a burden to him — they seemed like boring intervals, unbearable pauses, separating him from the purpose of his visits — from the tangible: some little feast, or some outing at their expense. He could not imagine acquaintance with women without ulterior motives. He kept a whole list of girls — how much dowry each had; nothing else interested him in that respect. Interest likewise determined his relations with his comrades. Flattery, slander, intrigues, and denunciations were the instruments of his advantage. Even things like national and tribal sympathies and antipathies served him only as a means of extracting personal gain. More than once he had dipped into the pockets of various Slavic committees, sometimes as “from Batak,” sometimes as an “emigrant.” But Aslanov is more of a master at those things.

Such was the exalted student who supported Bay Ganyo in his opinion of the foreigners’ egostopriemstvo. — Yes, we’re just soaking here in the cafés; nobody invites us to visit them — he repeated, to please Bay Ganyo.

— Well then, why do you want them to let you loaf around? — said a student with a bitter expression, smiling contemptuously; he evidently had long harbored hatred for the young egoist. — Do you want to be carried on their hands? Why? Because, not yet having managed to cross the threshold of their house, you will first flirt with the maid who meets you in the hallway? Because in their society you either keep silent like an oak, or open your mouth only to spout vulgarities and nonsense? Because to their faces you will praise them to the skies, and behind their backs you will slander them? Because you will throw dust in their eyes and present yourself as the son of a millionaire manufacturer or a shipowner, when your father has two charaks of braid-making thread or two broken crows’ nests—just so you can bewitch the parents and carry off their daughter? Why should they receive you with open arms? Who are you? What are you to them? In whose eyes are you thrusting your hospitality? And what is this much-vaunted hospitality of yours? — Is it that a Bulgarian will spread a greasy pallet for you and cover you with a dubious blanket? Ah, for God’s sake, enough of these savage boasts! Isn’t it time we opened our eyes already?
— What are you getting worked up about? Did you just now find the time to argue — one of the students chimed in — when we have a guest?

— Let the man have his say, he doesn’t want money, does he? — Bay Ganyo reassured him with this typical argument: “H e   d o e s n ’ t   w a n t   m o n e y!” He may say whatever he wants, do whatever he wants, as long as he doesn’t ask for money, as long as he doesn’t touch our pocket, our interests. He may even lie, he doesn’t want money!

But after this accidental incident, a friendly conversation could no longer be maintained. The company fell silent, and one after another they began to leave. Of the Bulgarians, only Bay Ganyo and the exalted student remained, who did not want to miss the chance to derive some benefit from his chance encounter with the Bulgarian rose-oil merchant.

— The pot rolled until it found its lid.

Not an hour had passed, and the student had managed to blacken his comrades so thoroughly before Bay Ganyo that he made him exclaim with all his heart: “Aferin, you scoundrels!” After another hour, Bay Ganyo was already in the student’s room, and the student skillfully exploited the guest’s arrival to his own advantage, introducing him to his landlords as his relative, a millionaire who “owns a whole heap of rose-oil factories.” He managed to borrow ten guilders from the landlady — to whom he had not paid the rent for the room for quite a long time. While in one room the student was extolling Bay Ganyo’s riches, in the neighboring room Bay Ganyo had already taken off his anteriya and was searching through it very carefully for something, muttering under his breath: “That cursed vermin has shown up again.”

The notion of cleanliness is not developed to a very high degree in Bay Ganyo. “Can a living person be without vermin?” — say the old people among us, and, reassured by this axiom, do not very zealously hinder the multiplication of the little creatures. And why should they deprive themselves of such a pleasure: the sun is shining hot, so what use is that sun if one cannot go out onto the porch, stretch out on the mat, sneeze two or three times from its dust, then have grandmother come, put one’s head on her knee, and she, with her bony fingers and mourning nails, dig into his hair and, as if shelling rice, begin: crack! — here, crack! — there, so that the creatures get frightened and start crawling over the head, and then there is a pleasant tickling, and grandmother starts singing, while that Balkan sun is blazing! Idyl...

Bai Ganyo, after finishing his entomological investigations, straightened up his attire and, without knocking, entered the neighboring room, but immediately exclaimed, “Pardon!”—and for good reason: he found the student and the landlady’s daughter in a very tender *vis-à-vis*—they had embraced each other, as befits two young loving hearts. The girl, ashamed, ran into the other room.
— Hey, why are you coming in like that? You’re embarrassing the girl — said the student with an ironic wink.
— You’ve hit the jackpot! — whispered Bay Ganyo mysteriously, his eyes shining like those of a monastery tomcat. — Shiny, the devil take it! Is she a maid?
— What a maid! The landlady’s daughter!

— Really? Here you can’t tell who is a maid and who is a mistress; they’re all polished up, all neatly dressed. If one of them steps out in front of you, grinning so sweetly and smoothly, you think she’s a maid, you tease her, and you bring trouble on your own head; if another appears, pretty and modest, you think, ah, this must be the mistress, you rise to your feet, invite her to sit down, she’s embarrassed — damn it! — you speak to her politely, and then you see her cleaning your boots!

From the student’s stories, accompanied by various gestures with which he embellished and gave greater force and meaning to his words, Bay Ganyo learned that for several months the young man had, under the guise of pure love, been attacking the widow’s daughter with irresistible persistence.

— And she, the wild one — the narrator explains, — hopes that I’ll take her as my wife! Let her hope, and let her feed me well, let her sew shirts for me. If she were some rich woman — I’d understand a man taking her, but she’s a pauper like me. She’s winding herself around me because she thinks I’m a rich man. If she knew what I really am, would she still be after me? The local women are terrible schemers! But I know how to handle them too, don’t I? — And he went on at length, explaining how he handled them...
— Bravo! — cried Bay Ganyo, with oily eyes, delighted by the young interlocutor.

— Wait a minute, is that all? If that’s all, then forget it! There’s another one, another one—I’ve got my eye on her, but who knows! If only I could turn her head—there’s something worth going after. Rich! I’ve been invited to their place tomorrow as a guest, and they’re going to take me to a village for a walk.
— Well, when are you going to take me to the factories? — asked the practical Bay Ganyo.

— Easy work, the day after tomorrow. You stay here tomorrow, hang around them; when they see that you don’t know the language, they won’t let you go to the inn, they’ll invite you to their place, and you’ll get a free meal.

And indeed, the next morning early the student went out visiting, and Bay Ganyo remained in the lodging alone with the hosts. As usual, that day too he got up very early, woke his companion and saw him off, and then waited a whole hour until the landladies woke up. This waiting was very hard for him; he felt some great need, like any person, but he forgot to ask the student where that thing was, and—whether he liked it or not—he had to wait for the household to get up and—shame or no shame—to ask them. It is very bad when a person does not know the language abroad; for the simplest thing they cannot understand you, and you always have to explain with your hands, with your fingers, to show them... But can everything be shown? Bay Ganyo knew languages: he could talk Turkish like a Turk, understood Romanian, and knew Serbian and Russian here and there, but the Germans and Czechs do not understand any of those languages. It cannot be said that Bay Ganyo did not know German at all; he knew a word or two.

In the neighboring room the ladies got up and began to bustle about. Bay Ganyo looked through the keyhole not out of any improper curiosity, but to see whether they were already dressed and, carefully, holding his breath, as he took in their attire, he was composing in his mind a phrase in German that would correspond to our: “Where is that thing for the big job?” — and at last, from the literal translation, he cobbled together the phrase: “Wo is diese fur gross Arbeit?” — Knock! knock! knock!
— Please! — called out two female voices from the neighboring room.
Bay Ganyo opened the door, said a “pardon,” and shyly uttered: — Wo is diese fur gross Arbeit? — and gestured with his fingers to emphasize the question.
— What, sir? — asked the girl in bewilderment, trying to make out the appearance of the millionaire recommended by her lover.
— For gross work? — repeated Bay Ganyo, even more embarrassed, and again gestured with his fingers and his head, but noticed that he had not been understood.
They understood him, but not as they should have; the women thought that he was telling them he had come to do big business, a large trade in rose oil.

“Damn the devil!” thinks Bay Ganyo. “What am I to do now?” — And so that at least the daughter would not witness his embarrassing predicament, he beckoned the mother into his room, closed the door, and, after repeating the question in German once more, this time added a desperate gesture that made the lady flee, choked with suppressed laughter, into the other room. The maid appeared and satisfied Bay Ganyo’s curiosity. A trio of unbroken female laughter shook the walls.

The aroma, wafting through the open kitchen door into the corridor, whetted Bay Ganyo’s appetite, and out of curiosity he peered in to see what they were cooking. There were the mistress of the house and the maid.

— What is that? — asked Bay Ganyo in a condescending tone, not so much out of a desire to get acquainted with the Czechs’ culinary art, as to show that he had been around Europe and knew these things, and that he could speak German too. — Soup, right? You’re making soup? I know. Ich versten supa!

And Bay Ganyo, with a mixture of German, Bulgarian, and mangled Bulgarian, aided by impressive gesticulations, made the landlady understand that he would not refuse to taste the fare of their kitchen. When he saw that the women showed a greater inclination to explain themselves in Czech, Bay Ganyo also switched to “Czech” and reinforced his condescending wish with the words: “ya khochem kushay,” which he interpreted by repeatedly touching his fingers to his open mouth, and then, pointing to his three fingers, he jabbed his chest with his index finger, jabbed the same finger toward the landlady’s chest, and a third time pointed into space, as though indicating the landlady’s invisible daughter, that is, “to eat together, the three of us!” It was also important for Bay Ganyo to know at what hour he would have lunch, since he intended to go for a walk so as not to miss the meal, and then “give money for food while there is free, blind luck,” and so he took out his huge watch and, holding it under the landlady’s nose, made her point with her finger at the hands to show him when he would “eat.” When he was convinced that everything was in order, Bay Ganyo went into his room, stuffed the little flasks into his belt, and went out into the street for a walk, and at the same time he would take a walk and perhaps run into some customer for rose oil.

Bai Ganyo looked around: many streets crossed here, one could easily take the wrong road, one could get lost, and, being a practical man, he glanced about to notice some sign by which he might recognize the house. He saw, on the opposite side, on a back wall, an inscription in large letters; he took out his notebook, moistened his pencil, copied the inscription exactly, and, fully convinced that he now had in his hands the most precise address of his lodgings, plunged into the narrow streets of old Prague. Now he would look at this, now at that, now here a customer, now there a customer; he got carried away, and not only got carried away, but lost his way altogether. What now? As he set out to look for his house, he got even more hopelessly tangled in the Jewish streets; an hour passed, then two hours passed, he would run into some house — no exit; he would take another direction, walk and walk, and suddenly come out on the bank of the Vltava. “Well, devil take it, what now?” And to make matters worse, lunchtime came — came and went. That Bai Ganyo trudged on and on, walked and walked, drenched to the skin, out of breath, looking like anything but himself. The people he met, especially the policemen, looked at him suspiciously, which only made him more confused. “Well, devil take it, what now?” And he was hungry too, his stomach in revolt, but why on earth should he throw his money to the wind when he had been invited to lunch?

But, you may ask, why is Bay Ganyo wandering about the streets when the address is in his pocket? Well, that’s the point! Bay Ganyo is no fool; do you think he did not think to take out his little notebook, stop one person after another in the street, and, pointing to the written address, ask them with his finger “which way”? He knows these things; he stops both men and women, but strangely enough — whoever he stops and asks, once he shows them what is written, they either look at him in astonishment and laugh, or turn away from him in indignation. One lady, probably some nervous old maid, when he showed her the address, snapped at him so sharply that even Bay Ganyo lost heart. “Well, damn it, either I’m crazy, or all Prague has gone mad,” he thinks to himself, and cannot stop wondering at the effect produced by his written address; while thinking, he keeps looking around, and then — isn’t this luck? — he sees before him Nàrodny Kavàrna, the café where Bulgarian students gather. Bay Ganyo goes in and finds the angry student.
— Good day! Tell me, your grace, am I the one who’s crazy, or are the people here crazy? — asks Bay Ganyo, out of breath, with wet hair plastered to his forehead.
The student looked at him questioningly. Bay Ganyo told him how he had gotten lost, how he had asked for his house by the address, and what they had answered him.
The student, knowing that the Czechs are rude and fanatical only toward the Germans, and otherwise quite polite, cannot help wondering how they could fail to do a favor for Bay Ganyo.
— Read it, please, what does it say here! — and Bay Ganyo handed over the little notebook.
The student read it: at first he frowned a little, then he burst out laughing!...
— Did you show this address to any lady? — he asked, laughing.
— Why? I showed it, didn’t I? Well?
— So? Do you know what is written here?
— What?
— It says “...Zde je zapovedeno...” “It is forbidden here to...” You copied it from some wall.
— Indeed! Look! T... t... t! Are you telling the truth? Look! — said Bay Ganyo, clicked his tongue a little, and then he too began to laugh.

The student did not know Bodkova’s lodging; they did not visit one another, and so he advised Bay Ganyo to wait, since some Bulgarian would surely come along and point out the house to him. It is easy to say “wait,” but let us see whether Bay Ganyo’s stomach was of the same opinion! And that it was not of the same opinion, he demonstrated it emphatically with an endless rumbling.
— Aren’t you hungry? — the student asked him, hearing the revolutionary signals.

— Me? — I’m not — lied old Ganyo a little, because if he told the truth, the other fellow would show him the inn, and he certainly did not want to admit to him (“How am I supposed to tell such a stubborn brat!”) that a profitable meal was waiting for him at the hosts’ place.

A conversation between Bay Ganyo and the “contrary little brat” could not get started. From their very first meeting, they somehow instinctively sensed that they were not made for each other, because, according to the Bulgarian proverb (ah, what exquisite proverbs the Bulgarian genius has created!) “mangy donkeys smell each other from nine hills away.” One had come from Bulgaria, the other had lived in Europe; they would surely have had something to talk about, since after all there must be some difference between the West and our fatherland. However, Bay Ganyo did not sense this difference, and how could he have sensed it! Wherever he went, he carried his own atmosphere, his own manners and customs with him; he looked for lodging according to his own tastes, met only his own kind of people, to whom he was accustomed and in whom, of course, he saw nothing new: if he went to Vienna, he would stay at the “London” hotel, where it was just as stuffy, just as full of kitchen smells and hydrogen sulfide as at home; he met the same Turks, Armenians, Serbs, and Albanians he was used to seeing every day; he would not go to Café “Habsburg,” because he was afraid they would fleece him, but would instead go again to the Greek café, which was just as dirty and stifling with perpetual smoke as our cafés are. If he went on business, he would go to the Bulgarian merchants, and through them he would not even realize that he was coming into contact with Europeans. And that it is precisely outside this limited sphere that European life begins, he neither knows nor, it seems, even wants to know. The education, the moral world of the European, his domestic setting — the product of centuries of tradition and gradual refinement, the intellectual movement, the social struggles and the way they are conducted, museums, libraries, philanthropic institutions, the fine arts, the thousands of manifestations of progress — do not burden Bay Ganyo’s attention.

“Because my father never did that either,” says Bay Ganyo, and, enchanted by this principle of petrification and ultra-retrogression, he is not too alarmed by the “new fashion,” that is, by civilization. But for all that, Bay Ganyo does not have the courage of the Chinese—to wall himself off with a wall against the invasion of civilization—and although he is inspired by the principle “my father never did this, and I won’t do it either,” you suddenly see that he has put on a clean shirt, put on gloves, and when they press him, he even puts on a frock coat; he grumbles, he laughs, but he puts on the frock coat. You hear him say “pardon,” talk about the “constitution,” boast here and there that he likes “soup,” when in fact he would prefer a spicy soup to all European dishes.
— Ah, here comes a little Bulgarian boy; he knows Bodkova’s lodging — declared the “stubborn little brat”...

— Come on, take me home — said Bay Ganyo to the little Bulgarian in a tone that ought to have disappeared even from our dealings with lazy servants; but the words “politeness,” “courtesy” are newly borrowed from the Russian language, “delicacy” is borrowed from the French, and among us the most suitable term for these notions is the word “mushiness.” These soft, gentle, heartfelt forms of address, which characterize the relations of civilized people and make life kinder, more pleasant — are incomprehensible to Bay Ganyo; he speaks as God gave him: “Come on, hey, listen, take me home.” And what does this mean: “I beg you, have the kindness, be so good as to...” what is all this mushiness!...

The Bulgarian boy led Bay Ganyo to the gate of his lodging and returned. Bay Ganyo looked at the unfortunate sign on the opposite wall, shook his head at it, clicked his tongue, and went into the house. In the corridor he met no one; he peeped into the kitchen — the fire there had already gone out, and the dishes were cleaned and put away. “Tsk, what a pity, I missed the chance” — muttered Bay Ganyo, went into his room, crouched over his saddlebags, took the little flasks out of his belt and stuffed them inside, pulled out the greasy cheese, cut himself a piece of dry bread, and began to stifle the revolution, munching so appetizingly that even the laziest Swiss cow would have envied him. To irritate his lymphatic organs, tired from unproductive labor, he let down his esophagus a chewed Arnaut pepper, which brought tears to his eyes and made him accompany his munching with sniffles. The maid, who was bustling in the neighboring room, hearing the strange sounds with which Bay Ganyo accompanied his breakfast, opened the door and peeped into the room: Bay Ganyo shyly hid the saddlebags behind his back, turned his tearful and sweaty face, said “pardon!”, sniffed vigorously through his nose, and drove the maid away — that is, not that he told her to go out, but she hurried to run off, thinking that the millionaire might have received some sad news.

Bodkov did not return that evening. Toward evening the hosts came back; a fire was lit again in the kitchen and they began to prepare supper. Bay Ganyo already considers himself on familiar terms, “well, after all, with women what’s there to stand on ceremony for?” says he, and without any preamble walks into the kitchen and explains, more with gestures than with words, that he had lost his way in the streets and missed lunch, but never mind — he is due one lunch, and he will make it up with one supper. Bay Ganyo also understands the culinary art, and not only does he understand it, but every violation of that craft enrages him. He saw, for example, that the hostess was about to put a fresh fish into the boiling water, and he rose up with all his energy, seized the hostess’s hand, pulled the fish out with the other hand, and made a sign with his hand and head, meaning: “Stop, don’t move, just watch how fish is cooked!” “Salt!” commands Bay Ganyo. They give him salt; he rolls up his sleeves to the elbows on his hairy arms, reaches into the saltcellar with his not exactly delicate fingers, and begins to salt and rub the already salted fish on the outside and inside. “Red pepper!” — but where would those savages have red pepper! “Black pepper” — commands Bay Ganyo, grabs the pepper, and rubs it over the fish. “Grill!” — trumpets the triumphant cook, but here they could not understand him, despite all his gestures, and he himself looked around and could not spot a grill; but is that an obstacle for Bay Ganyo? He is no yesterday’s man! Taking the tongs, he raked all the fire toward the opening of the oven, left the other dishes to rest (which was just as well, since they were already ready), spread the tongs apart, placed the fish on them, and tried to shove it into the oven, but the little door was narrow, the fish caught, slipped, and — splat! — into the fire. “Ah!” cried the hostess. “Nothing, nothing!” Bay Ganyo reassured her, grabbed the fish, blew off the clinging coals and ash, and put it back on the grill. Smoke and the smell of fish filled the whole kitchen. The hostesses were in despair; Bay Ganyo was radiant — he was now in his element; while grilling the fish he blew and sniffed, irritated by the appetizing smoke, and with his free hand, smeared from turning the fish, he commanded them to set the table so that his dish would not grow cold: “Fresh fish isn’t hot — throw it on!” The fish, roasted, with its tail and head rolled in ash, was placed on a plate, and at Bay Ganyo’s polite command: “Quick! Quick! While it’s hot, bring lemon and wine; without wine it’s not worth two cents!” — they sat down around the table, sending the maid running for lemon and wine. What could they do! The millionaire was not going to change his habits for their pleasure, after all! The hostess reached to cut the fish. “Please, please, please! For heaven’s sake!” cried Bay Ganyo and grabbed her hand; then he turned the fish over onto its back, pressed here and there with his two fingers, and it split into two halves. Well, now, who wouldn’t triumph? The maid brought the lemon; Bay Ganyo cut it, took half in a whole handful, and squeezed it over the plate with such care that even the fleshy parts of the lemon fell onto the fish. What do you think, doesn’t Bay Ganyo have an appetite? Hardly as much lemon juice flowed into the plate as saliva Bay Ganyo swallowed. And wine was brought. Supper began.

Carlsbad and I don’t know what other -bad they recommend the Aesculapians to those suffering from catarrh of the stomach. Let them take these sufferers by the ear and place them at the table before Bay Ganyo, and then let their stomachs be upset even more than the streets of Yuchbunar... you’ll see what effect the spectacle will have on them!... Bay Ganyo is eating, boy, he’s not joking, he’s eating so hard his ears flap! All the organs of his body are in motion, and first of all his teeth, tongue, and nose. Here one realizes the poverty and inadequacy of language! With what words, with what interjections, with what punctuation marks, and finally with what musical notes is it possible to depict those smacking, grunting, sniffing, clattering, clicking, sucking sounds that pour out of Bay Ganyo like hail!... Lucky are the hostesses! Not every Czech woman will have the good fortune to enjoy such a spectacle.

They had finally eaten. They went into the drawing room. Bay Ganyo, red as a peony, kept twirling his little mustache, kept clearing his throat with his hand, and kept muttering “pardon.” They settled into the chairs. Bay Ganyo rolled a cigarette, greasy from his fingers, and began to puff and blow clouds of smoke through his mustache. Is this not the most fitting moment for enjoyment: for music, for songs, for love? The girl caught the millionaire’s mood and asked him whether he liked music. Who? Bay Ganyo? Why, if Bay Ganyo does not like music, who else would? Who else has been able to inspire such respect in the Gypsies, that is, in the musicians, as Bay Ganyo? Just let him wink at them, and look what happens to those Gypsies! Fire! Fire! Twist that violin of yours, squeal that clarinet of yours!
Your figure is like a poplar,
on my heart like two stakes.
On your dress, I’m dragging.
burn my liver...

— Enough, you scoundrel! I don’t want any love songs! Play me some rakia music! — cried Bay Ganyo to them and clapped his glass on the table. They start “Karan-karanfiltcheto,” Bay Ganyo claps his glass, they stop. They start “We do not desire wealth” — he claps his glass again. They turn to “Green little leaf.” “Ha, did you see that now! Ahhh! Now we’re having fun, now!”... — and he smashes the bottle on the ground or in the window... Well, who’s the master of these things? And was it once, was it twice? But h o w   c a n   t h o s e   w o m e n   k n o w   who your Uncle Ganyo is! And even if you tell them how many panes you’ve broken with music, they still can’t understand!...

— I love music! — said Bay Ganyo condescendingly. — I love music! — he repeated and shook his head, which in his opinion expressed the sad necessity of having to listen, for the women’s sake, to some miserable tinkling on the piano. “What do you understand about playing, about conversation?” Bay Ganyo thought to himself.

The girl opened the piano and began playing one endless piece after another from *The Bartered Bride* by Smetana. Under her fingers there poured forth the sounds that bring every Czech soul to ecstasy. Her mother, who was probably hearing those pieces for the thousand-and-first time, was steeped in bliss, and in her gaze, turned toward Bay Ganyo, national pride and self-satisfaction shone; she kept her head in time with the tempo of the piece, now adagio, now allegro, as though punctuating the notes of the flourishes with her nose. From time to time she would signal to Bay Ganyo with her eyes, warning him of the approach of some favorite moment in the piece, and the millionaire would reply: “Mind you, your grace, don’t look at me—how many times I’ve heard them a z t a k v i z!...” And in order to back up this sign with action, he rose from his chair precisely at the moment when the hostess expected to revel in the effect Smetana would produce on Bay Ganyo, and hurriedly, with a plan in his head, went to his room, took from his saddlebags the muskal of rose oil he had opened for testing, and returned to the drawing room, winked at the mother: “watch what will have an effect,” tiptoed up to the girl, absorbed in the music, and—what a terrible devil that Bay Ganyo was!—opened the muskal of rose oil and gently shoved it under the girl’s nose. She, upon feeling the breath of Bay Ganyo’s sweaty hand, stinking of fish, turned away in disgust and, carried away by the music, at first glanced at him with a frown, but immediately came to her senses that the millionaire was standing before her and grinning, and asking her: “Which do you like better, your Smetana, or this thing you just smelled, eh?”—and he tucked the muskal into his sash...

The girl stopped playing. Bay Ganyo began...

(What did you say?—I couldn’t understand you!)...

He began to play carelessly with one finger, without sitting down at the chair: “Just enough to let these people know that we too understand a little about these vajiis.” In one of Bay Ganyo’s relatives’ houses there had turned up a little hand harmonica with keys, so every now and then, when he felt like it, Bay Ganyo would break his fingers trying to pick out some tune. Now he began a startled pizzicato, which in his opinion represented the song: “Stole-la,” say, granny’s, sla-slanin-kaaa, bacon, stole granny’s bacon... which “Slaninka” is entirely stolen from the Czech “Slaninka.”
— Pan is playing “Slaninka,” mama! — the girl announced her discovery.
— “Slaninka,” sir — said Bay Ganyo, — how do you know it?

Delighted by his success, Bay Ganyo sat down on the chair to play, now quite reasonably, something more serious. And what could be more serious than “The Night Is Terrible”? Bay Ganyo began to play, but he himself remained dissatisfied with the performance. And quite naturally! “The Night Is Terrible” was not created for the piano; the sounds get cut off: you press the key for “terr-i-i-ble!” and the voice is cut short; a harmonica is another matter! Once you put your finger on “... terr-i-i-ble...” — press away, damn it! Let it drone for half an hour, press, bend it in waves, until you feel like it! But with the piano — bang, bang, nothing! Bay Ganyo saw that the effect produced by “The Little Bacon” would weaken, thought and thought, and then decided: “Well, wait, let me sing ‘The Night Is Terrible’ to these women!...” He pondered a bit, wanted to get into a sad mood, in the spirit of the mournful song, sighed deeply once, put his right hand to his ear, half-closed his eyes, and when he opened his mouth!...

“Grandissimo maestro Verdi! You have no enemies, you cannot have enemies! But if, against all expectations, some monster were to appear, it would be the devil himself. God is great, Esimio Maestro! — and all the arrows of the evil spirit are powerless against you! Only one thing... only one means can the cunning one use, and the whole musical world will be covered in mourning... We shall pray, and you too pray, Divin Maestro, to the almighty Creator not to allow Satan to lead you into the hall where Bay Ganyo sings ‘Night is terrible’... And when your most delicate hearing is shaken by the wild, inhuman sounds incomprehensible to you, may the Evil Spirit reveal the terrible truth to you with his satanic laughter: Ha! ha! ha! Verdi! This is a song from your   d i v i n e   ‘Traviata’! Ha! ha! ha! ha-a!!...”
— It’s already late, gentlemen — said the shy Ilcho, glancing at his watch, — midnight! Let’s go home, and another time, God willing, we’ll talk again about Bay Ganyo.

— Hey, Ilcho, tell me, why do you hate Bulgarian songs so much? — Dravichkata asked as they were leaving. — Who? Me, hate them? Sorry, my dear, if you misunderstood me. I am capable of admiring, of losing myself, of being carried away to ecstasy by our beautiful melancholic folk songs, but by Bulgarian songs, not by those disgusting parodies of foreign vulgar songs that our Bay Ganyo types hand down to us, twisted beyond recognition through those gypsy appoggiaturas and throat-ripping embellishments with drunken trills and flourishes... We have songs, but we have no singers. I am ready to embrace my enemy if he sings to me properly the song “Bogdane, may God strike you dead” or “Come on, Velo girl, roll up your white sleeves,” and to look askance at my friend when I see him admiring “Green Little Leaf,” “The Little Carnation,” and other such gypsy delights...
